title: Using a fungal biomarker test to help decide when to stop antifungal treatment in intensive care patients
official: Antifungals - stopping early with a fungal biomarker-based stewardship algorithm in critical care
summary:
Background and study aims
Patients in ICUs are often given antifungal medicines when a serious fungal infection is suspected. Current lab tests are slow and doctors do not have high confidence in them. Because delays in treatment can increase the risk of death doctors usually start antifungal treatment before results are available. This means up to 95% of patients receiving these medicines do not have a fungal infection. The treatment is costly, can cause side effects, and over‑use contributes to drug resistance. Reducing unnecessary treatment would benefit both patients and the NHS.
We want to test new rapid blood tests in addition to standard care testing. These tests are not widely used in the NHS because it is unclear whether they improve patient care or offer good value for money. Previous research assessed four biomarker tests and identified two that reliably rule out fungal infection when added to standard tests. We now want to see whether using these two tests can safely reduce unnecessary antifungal treatment.

Who can participate?
Adults in intensive care who may have a fungal infection caused by Candida.

What does the study involve?
If someone is eligible for the study, a small blood sample will be taken when they are first identified as a possible participant. For people in the treatment group, this sample will be tested in a laboratory. The test result will be used to provide doctors with advice about whether antifungal medication should be stopped or continued.
The doctors looking after the participant will make the final decision about treatment and do not have to follow this advice if they feel a different approach is best.
Participants will also be asked to complete a short questionnaire about three months after joining the study.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Taking part may not directly benefit participants. However, the information gained from the study could help improve care for future patients.
We do not expect there to be any additional risks from taking part in this study.

Where is the study run from? 
The study is being coordinated by the Warwick Clinical Trials Unit at the University of Warwick and is overseen by Queen's University Belfast.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
The study is expected to start recruiting participants in December 2026 and recruitment is planned to continue until June 2030.

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR).

Who is the main contact?
For further details contact Sara Wood on A-Stop2@warwick.ac.uk

interventions.name:
Patients will be randomly assigned to one of two groups;
1 - treatment recommendations based on biomarker results.
2 - Standard NHS care as the control arm

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	Adults (age >=18 years) in ICU (level 2/3)
2.	Prescribed antifungal therapy for suspected Candida infection
Exclusion criteria:
1.	More than 48hrs of systemic antifungal treatment in the preceding 7 days 
2.	Antifungal treatment started for suspected non-Candida fungal infection (e.g. aspergillus) 
3.	Neutropenia (< 0.5x10^9/L)
4.	Receiving immunosuppressant therapy for organ transplant
5.	Previous randomisation in the present trial
6. Persons currently serving a custodial sentence in a prison setting (e.g., Her Majesty’s Prison or equivalent) are excluded. This does not apply to individuals temporarily held in police custody
